teaser: The most famous book of the Middle Ages was abandoned half done. Its painters never saw it bound.

lesson.text: This book is a failure, at least by the standard of the men who started it. Around 1411 three brothers from Nijmegen, Paul, Herman and Jean de Limbourg, began painting a prayer book for a French prince. In 1416 all three died, none of them older than thirty or so. Their patron died the same year. The pages lay loose and unfinished.

The prince was Jean, Duke of Berry, brother of one king of France and uncle of the next. He collected castles, rubies, exotic animals and, above all, books. A “book of hours” was a private prayer book for people who were not priests, with prayers set for each hour of the day. He already owned several. This one was meant to outshine them all.

Every book of hours opens with a calendar, one page per month. The brothers turned those twelve pages into twelve full paintings. You are looking at January, the first. In the complete page an arch of sky with the signs of the zodiac sits above this scene. Below it, a party is in full swing. Somewhere in this crowd sits the man who paid for everything.

lesson.title: Finding the host
lesson.text: More than twenty people fill the room. The painters use three tricks to tell you which one matters.

spots.title: A halo of wicker
spots.text: The round shape behind the man in the fur hat is a woven screen that shields him from the fireplace at his back. It also frames his head like a saint's halo. This is the Duke.

spots.title: His signs overhead
spots.text: The red canopy carries blue discs with gold fleurs-de-lis, the lilies of the French royal family, and white swans. The swan was one of the Duke's personal emblems, stamped on what he owned.

spots.title: The costliest blue
spots.text: His robe is painted with ultramarine, a blue made by grinding lapis lazuli, a stone carried from the mountains of Afghanistan. It cost about as much as gold.

lesson.text: So the Duke had himself painted into his own prayer book, bigger than his guests and wrapped in the most expensive color on the page. Nobody found that odd. A book like this was a prayer aid, and also a mirror held up to its owner.

The brothers knew how to tease their employer. On New Year's Day 1411 they gave the Duke a splendid book that turned out to be a block of wood, painted to look like a volume bound in white velvet with silver clasps. He kept it in his collection.

January 1st was the day for gifts at a French court, the way Christmas is in many homes today. The feast you see is that day. Courtiers arrive with presents and hope for bigger ones in return. One man in the picture has the job of waving them forward, and the painters did something almost unheard of: they wrote down what he says.
Two words float in the air, written in gold. Can you spot them?

spots.title: “Aproche, aproche”
spots.text: “Come closer, come closer.” The official below, staff over his shoulder, is calling the guests toward the Duke. It works like a speech bubble, five and a half centuries before comic strips.

lesson.text: With that call in your ear, the picture starts to move. The crowd on the left pushes in from the cold. Two men lift their palms toward the warmth of the fire. At the table, servants carve and pour. The brothers painted a still image and filled it with small verbs.
A medieval calendar page shows a month by what people do in it. January means feasting and gifts indoors; later months show plowing, harvest and the hunt.

Now lift your eyes above the heads. The soldiers up there are not in the room. They belong to a tapestry hanging on the wall, a woven picture as large as a building's facade. Tapestries were the true luxury of the age, worth far more than paintings, and the Duke owned dozens.

lesson.title: A room built from treasure
lesson.text: Each thing here was a real kind of object the Duke's clerks listed in his inventories.

spots.title: War in wool
spots.text: Knights in steel-blue armor charge with lances under bright banners. The lines of text woven along the top suggest the story is the Trojan War, retold in the armor of 1400.

spots.title: The gold on show
spots.text: A sideboard is stacked with gold jugs, cups and dishes. Nobody eats from them. Plate was displayed during a feast the way a bank displays its vault.

spots.title: The cupbearer
spots.text: This young man in a long blue coat holds a shallow cup. Serving the prince's wine was an honor reserved for the well born, and he dresses like it.

lesson.text: All that gold is real gold. The page is vellum, fine calfskin scraped until it is smooth as paper. Gold leaf was laid down first and polished, then colors mixed with gum were added with brushes of a few hairs. The whole page is roughly 29 by 21 centimeters, about 11 by 8 inches. Many faces are smaller than a fingernail.

Some scholars think the brothers slipped themselves into the party. The usual candidate is a guest in a floppy grey cap in the crowd on the left. No document confirms it, which has never stopped anyone from looking.
The feast is also full of animals behaving badly, and the painters clearly enjoyed that. Go and look for them yourself, along with the people who keep this party running.

spots.title: Dogs on the table
spots.text: Two tiny lapdogs walk across the white cloth and help themselves from the dishes. Nobody shoos them away. They were the Duke's pets.

spots.title: The greyhound
spots.text: A white hound with a red collar lies on the floor, fed by a servant who is mostly cut off by the edge.

spots.title: The carver
spots.text: In a green patterned coat with a white towel over his shoulder, he slices meat at the table. A knife case hangs from his belt.

spots.title: A churchman
spots.text: The man in red with a white fur collar is a high-ranking cleric, thanking his host with a hand on his chest. He sits at the Duke's own table, a rare favor.

spots.title: Cold hands
spots.text: Newcomers raise their open palms toward the fire. It is the only hint in the whole picture that this is winter.

spots.title: Fashion parade
spots.text: A twisted blue headdress, a mauve hood, a scarlet hat. Court clothes around 1400 were bright, costly and competitive.

spots.title: The floor
spots.text: The golden ground is woven rush matting, the ordinary floor covering of a rich house. The painters drew its plaited pattern strand by strand.

lesson.text: Then, 1416. The Duke died in June, deep in debt, and the three brothers were dead before the year was out, possibly from an epidemic. The unbound pages passed from hand to hand. Around the 1440s an unknown painter worked on some of them. In the 1480s the Duke of Savoy hired Jean Colombe to finish the job, some seventy years after it began.
The Très Riches Heures was made by at least three teams across three generations. January is the brothers' own work, painted for a man who would never turn the finished pages.

After that the book vanished from view for centuries. In 1856 a French prince in exile, the Duke of Aumale, was shown it at a girls' school near Genoa and bought it for 18,000 francs. He took it home to his château at Chantilly and gave it the name it still carries, the “Very Rich Hours.”

You can travel to Chantilly and still not see this page. Aumale left his collection to France on the condition that nothing ever be lent, and the book is so fragile that it is almost never opened to the public. Most visitors meet a facsimile, an exact printed copy.

quiz.question: What happened to the book in 1416?
options: Its painters and its patron died, leaving it unfinished
It was stolen from the Duke
quiz.explanation: The three Limbourg brothers and the Duke of Berry all died that year, and the pages stayed loose.

quiz.question: What is the round shape behind the Duke's head?
options: A wicker screen protecting him from the fire
quiz.explanation: It is a woven fire screen that the painters also use to frame him like a halo.

quiz.question: What do the gold words “aproche, aproche” mean?
quiz.explanation: An official is calling the guests forward to the Duke.

quiz.question: Where are the charging knights at the top?
options: In a tapestry hanging on the wall
quiz.explanation: They belong to a huge woven wall hanging, the costliest decoration of the time.

quiz.question: What is the page made of?
quiz.explanation: The brothers painted on vellum with gold leaf and colors mixed with gum.

quiz.question: Who had the book completed in the 1480s?
options: The Duke of Savoy, who hired Jean Colombe
quiz.explanation: Jean Colombe finished it for the Duke of Savoy about seventy years after it was begun.

facts.text: The Limbourg brothers once gave the Duke a fake book made of painted wood.
facts.explanation: It was their New Year's gift in 1411, and he kept it.

facts.text: The blue of the Duke's robe was a cheap color made from local plants.
facts.explanation: It is ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli and about as costly as gold.

facts.text: The Musée Condé regularly lends the manuscript to museums around the world.
facts.explanation: The Duke of Aumale's bequest forbids lending anything from Chantilly.
